item.text: {"question_id":"8B.7","answer":"For the 2023 target period, outcomes moved toward some objectives but the portfolio result was mixed and not consistently attributable to López Obrador. The strongest favorable evidence is the 2018–2022 decline in multidimensional poverty from 41.9% to 36.3%, a CONEVAL counterfactual indicating that social transfers reduced 2022 poverty from an estimated 39.0% to 36.3% and extreme poverty from 8.9% to 7.1%, and expanded older-person pension coverage and benefits. These results are relevant to the administration’s transfer and poverty objectives, but they are lagged outcomes observed through 2022, not a 2023-only measure, and the counterfactual combines transfers from all levels of government rather than isolating the presidency (BATCH-0032-E002; BATCH-0032-E009; BATCH-0032-E006). The favorable movement also reflected higher minimum wages, labor income, remittances, and post-pandemic recovery, while the World Bank identifies the pandemic, U.S. recovery, nearshoring, low productivity, and subdued investment as important contextual factors (BATCH-0050-E003; BATCH-0052-E014). Distributional progress was incomplete: poverty declined overall, but extreme poverty increased in absolute terms from 8.7 to 9.1 million people; vulnerability by social deprivation and severe deprivation increased; Indigenous and disabled populations retained much higher poverty and deprivation; and health-access deprivation rose from 16.2% in 2018 to 39.1% in 2022, with especially severe effects in lower-income groups (BATCH-0032-E002; BATCH-0032-E003; BATCH-0032-E007). Public healthcare use remained below 2018 levels and catastrophic health spending rose from 2.1% to 2.9%, although the source identifies pandemic effects, survey changes, and institutional transition as qualifying explanations (BATCH-0032-E010). Security outcomes provide no clear attributable advance: some reported crime measures fell from 2018 to 2023, but crime rose from 2022 to 2023, justice-system capacity deteriorated, impunity remained above 90%, and the supplied subnational analysis found no consistent association between greater National Guard activity and homicide reduction, with measurement and alternative local explanations remaining plausible (BATCH-0016-E008; BATCH-0016-E009; BATCH-0016-E010; BATCH-0016-E011). Infrastructure progress was observable but incomplete and costly at the end of 2023: the Maya Train opened only partially, with delays, unfinished facilities and connections, major cost escalation, limited access, and benefits not yet demonstrated (BATCH-0030-E004; BATCH-0011-E006). Thus, the evidence supports partial movement toward poverty-reduction, transfer, labor-income, and possibly security objectives, but substantial adverse distributional and service outcomes, incomplete flagship-project results, realistic lag, shocks, inherited conditions, subnational responsibility, and weak causal isolation prevent treating 2023 outcomes as broad or clearly ruler-produced goal
